o1.biggest_strength: Separates proved from to-check with an owner, a deadline and a method on every open question, and it names the tracking gap (Meta's purchase count versus store orders since the January move) that decides whether Meta's $121 is real.
o1.biggest_mistake: It ranks the moves on a soft High/Medium impact label instead of gross profit, and leaves the board's headline metric as 'set baseline in week 1 / up every month', so the scorecard has no contribution number to manage against.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Put each move in one unit (points of contribution on revenue, with the working) and give the contribution scorecard a baseline and a week-13 target instead of 'up every month'.

o2.biggest_strength: It converts everything into one currency - points of contribution on revenue - derives a 7.8% baseline and 11% week-13 target with the working shown, and gives each move a decision threshold, a holdout and an owner, so the plan can actually be run on a Monday.
o2.biggest_mistake: The Meta sizing is about $2 light: at $110/$100/$90 per first order the share-weighted blended cost is roughly $101/$95/$90, not $99/$94/$89, and its tracking check never compares platform purchase counts to store orders, which is the gap that would prove or disprove the Meta number.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Fix the blended-cost arithmetic and add the platform-versus-store order gap check, while keeping the one-unit ranking and the act-when triggers.

reason: Both diagnose the same three leaks correctly, but output 2 answers the actual ask - moves ranked in gross profit with a real contribution baseline, target and act-when triggers - where output 1 gives impact as High/Medium and a scorecard with no contribution number; output 1 is the easier read and catches the tracking gap, so it is close, but I would pay more for the one I can hand to the team and run.
